source_text:
Cogitanti mihi et cum animo meo Octaui boni et fidelissimi contubernalis memoriam recensenti tanta dulcedo et adfectio hominis inhaesit, ut ipse quodammodo mihi uiderer in praeterita redire, non ea quae iam transacta et decursa sunt, recordatione reuocare:
ita eius contemplatio quantum subtracta est oculis, tantum pectori meo ac paene intimis sensibus inplicata est.
nec inmerito decedens uir eximius et sanctus inmensum sui desiderium nobis reliquit, utpote cum et ipse tanto nostri semper amore flagrauerit, ut et in ludicris et seriis pari mecum uoluntate concineret eadem uelle uel nolle: crederes unam mentem in duobus fuisse diuisam.
sic solus in amoribus conscius, ipse socius in erroribus: et cum discussa caligine de tenebrarum profundo in lucem sapientiae et ueritatis emergerem, non respuit comitem, sed quod est gloriosius, praecucurrit.
itaque cum per uniuersam conuictus nostri et familiaritatis aetatem mea cogitatio uolueretur, m illo praecipue sermone eius mentis meae resedit intentio, quo Caecilium superstitiosis uanitatibus etiamnunc inhaerentem disputatione grauissima ad ueram religionem reformauit.
thought_title: The memory of Octavius and his winning of Caecilius
orientation: Marcus, the narrator, opens the dialogue by recalling his dear friend Octavius and the debate in which Octavius converted Caecilius to true religion.
pass_a_gloss: As I was thinking and with my mind recalling the memory of Octavius, a good and most faithful companion, so great a sweetness and affection for the man clung to me, that I myself in some way seemed to me to return into past things, not to call back by recollection those things which are already finished and run through: so much as the contemplation of him was withdrawn from my eyes, so much was it entwined into my breast and almost into my innermost senses. And not undeservedly did the departing man, extraordinary and holy, leave to us an immense longing for himself, since he himself always burned with so great a love of us, that both in playful things and in serious things he agreed with me with equal will, to want or not want the same things: you would believe one mind had been divided in two. Thus he alone was a sharer in my loves, he himself a partner in my wanderings: and when, after the fog was scattered, I was emerging from the depth of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth, he did not reject me as a companion, but, what is more glorious, he ran on ahead. And so, when my thought was turning over the whole span of our life together and our friendship, my mind's attention settled especially on that discourse of his, by which he reformed Caecilius, still clinging to superstitious vanities, to true religion by a most weighty disputation.

choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'superstition' in adjectival form and renders uanitatibus literally as 'vanities' to preserve the dismissive tone.
Uses the glossary term 'religion' and renders ueram literally as 'true' to match the contrast with superstition.

choices.english: the light of wisdom and truth
choices.why: Uses the glossary terms 'wisdom' and 'truth' and keeps the metaphor of light literally.
rejected: the light of insight and reality

choices.term: unam mentem in duobus fuisse diuisam
choices.english: one mind had been divided in two
choices.why: Renders the perfect passive infinitive literally to preserve the vivid hypothetical statement.
rejected: one soul shared between two bodies

choices.why: Renders grauissima literally as 'most weighty' to convey the seriousness of the argument.

pass_b_english: As I was thinking and going over in my mind the memory of Octavius, my good and most faithful companion, such sweetness and affection for the man clung to me that I seemed in some way to return to the past, not merely to call back by recollection things already finished and run their course.
His image, the more it has been withdrawn from my eyes, the more it is entwined with my heart and almost with my innermost feelings.

And not without reason did that extraordinary and holy man, when he departed, leave behind an immense longing for himself in us, since he himself always burned with so great a love for us that in both playful and serious matters he agreed with me in equal desire, wanting and not wanting the same things: you would have believed one mind had been divided in two.

He alone was the confidant in my loves, the companion in my errors; and when the fog was scattered and I was emerging from the depths of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth, he did not refuse to be my companion, but, what is more glorious, he ran on ahead.

And so, as my thought wandered through the whole span of our life together and our friendship, my mind's attention settled especially on that discourse of his by which he converted Caecilius, who was still clinging to superstitious vanities, to true religion by a most weighty disputation.

problems.quote: since he himself always burned with so great a love for me
problems.source_quote: utpote cum et ipse tanto nostri semper amore flagrauerit
problems.why: Latin says his love was for "nostri" (us), not just the narrator; English narrows agency to "me".
problems.fix: since he himself always burned with so great a love for us
problems.ruling: nostri = 'of us' (objective genitive), not 'me'; English 'for me' misrepresents mutual love between friends.

edits.old: since he himself always burned with so great a love for me
edits.new: since he himself always burned with so great a love for us

fixed: Changed 'for me' to 'for us' because the source 'nostri' means 'of us', not just the narrator.

polish.changed: Clarified that the narrator is speaking throughout, kept the single paragraph as one continuous reflection, and removed the em dash by recasting the clause about Octavius running ahead.

notes.why: The pagan opponent is called Caecilius in most sections but addressed as Marcus in others, confusing the reader about identity.
notes.fix: Standardize the name to Caecilius or explain that Marcus is his praenomen.

notes.why: Octavius is suddenly called 'Januarius' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Januarius is an alternate name for Octavius.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.
